Chirality desktop · shell review · round 3 · 2026-09-04

One shell, three panels, one dialogue

Stone only. No header row. The left panel is where chats are kept and organised. The centre is the dialogue and it never leaves. The right panel is everything else, one view at a time: files, an open document, who is working, activity, a child session. The walkthrough tab clicks through it.

Chirality, in one page

A desktop application in which a person directs AI agents inside their own folders, under permissions they set, along roadmaps that stop at the decisions that are theirs. It is the runtime for a method: decomposition, roles, governed workflows, and a record. The method arrives through a consulting engagement and stays behind as files the organisation owns.

The human declares

Every chat says where it works, with which agent, under what permission, and how much delegation. Nothing is promoted silently; every step up is a deliberate act, proposed by the agent or chosen by you.

The agent proposes, the record binds

Agents answer, draft, and propose. Deterministic tools compute. Decisions are yours and are written against the exact content you decided on. Output is never confused with authority.

Files are the truth

Workflows, roadmaps, and records live in your folder, under your version control. No database, no tenancy, nothing you cannot read without the app.

How work moves

Open a folder, ask

A plain chat with Help, the default agent. Any folder, structured or not. Ask, read, summarise, draft.

steps 1–7

Documents beside the chat

Files open in the side panel. Replies cite documents as chips; a selection in a document becomes a quote in your message.

steps 2–7

The work earns a role

When a question is an Agent 1's work, Help proposes the specified chat: folder, agent, permission, delegation. Accept, adjust, or not now.

steps 21–22

A procedure becomes a workflow

The Agent 1 recognises its own protocol and proposes a governed workflow: a roadmap with your gates marked, briefs run by bounded agents, on the local model if you have one.

steps 23–24

Steps, gates, decisions

The agent works a step, stops at a gate, and says so. The current step is always in view. You accept or decline; the app records it against the content.

steps 18–19

The record stays

Every session, child run, proposal, and decision is in the folder. Replay any child. Bind the workflow to the next folder. The method keeps applying itself.

steps 8–9, 16–17

Salient features

One dialogue, never displaced

The centre is the interface with the agent and it never leaves. Everything else is a side panel, one view at a time.

SR-01 · steps 1–4

The specification tuple

Folder, agent, permission, delegation, roadmap. Shown under the message at all times; declared per chat; fixed for a workflow.

SR-21–24 · step 16

The prompted ladder

Plain chat → specified chat → governed workflow. The agent offers each rung once when the work earns it; declines are remembered and recorded; the direct route is the same form.

SR-24 · steps 21–25

Governed workflows as files

A roadmap tied to an Agent 1 role, living in the folder, steering the chat by context injection and never holding the record. Library and Bind carry it to the next folder.

SR-23 · steps 16–20

Human gates, recorded

Roadmap steps that are yours are marked. The agent stops there. Your decision is written against the content hash you saw.

step 19

Woven both ways

Replies cite documents as chips that open beside the chat. Selections in documents quote into the message with file and lines.

SR-09 · steps 5–7

Agent 0 aligns, Agent 2 executes

Help holds no write scope and keeps its context on you. Bounded briefs do the work, on a local model when available. Every child is visible and replayable.

steps 8–9

Permissions you can feel

Read only, ask before changes, approve each write, run bounded briefs. Consent and permissions are per folder; the account is app-wide.

SR-19 · steps 12–15

Private by construction

Folders never leave the machine unless you say so. A local model runs delegated work with nothing sent anywhere.

steps 13–14

Written for people who do not code

Plain language everywhere: no identifiers, no subtitles, no disclaimers in the body. Tool calls read as sentences.

SR-18

What the service leaves behind

  • Workflows in each folder: roadmaps tied to roles, with the protocol version they were derived from, so the app can say when one is behind the method.
  • Agents and skills in an organisation layer over the bundled instruction root, owned by the client, hash-pinned.
  • The record: sessions, child runs, proposals offered and declined, decisions at gates. Evidence for the client's own duty of care, and for the follow-up.
  • The habit: the ladder keeps proposing the method after the consultant has gone.

What it refuses to do

  • Promote a chat, create a workflow, or pass a gate without a human act.
  • Let an agent's capability become authority. Better models draft better; they do not decide.
  • Hold project truth anywhere but the folder.
  • Create a workflow with any of the declarations missing.
  • Ask twice. One proposal per chat per trigger.

The twenty-second demonstration is the Walkthrough tab: a plain question, a proposal, a roadmap with a gate, a decision recorded.

Applied from your review

  • No header row. "Chirality" sits at the top of the left panel, Plex Serif in the dark umber; the icon lives in the Dock and the corporate lockup. The working-root chip, the status chip, and the gear are gone: the folder is chosen in the composer, the strip already shows status, and Settings is in the account popover.
  • Stone only. Linen and the umber navigator are dropped. Colour is the wordmark and the accents that mean "this is live" or "this is a document".
  • Three panels with a rank. Centre is primary and always present. Left is secondary: chat history, search, groups, pins. Right is tertiary: one view at a time from Files, Who is working, Activity, plus an open document or a child session when you select one.
  • Message on its own line. The box holds only the message, attach, and send. The folder, agent, and permission level sit under the box as a sentence: \'Working in chirality-app-dev · Working Items · Ask before changes\', each part a selector. A new chat starts with \'Start in\' and the folder and agent live; after the first message the folder is fixed for that chat. The left panel lists chats from every folder with the folder shown under each title.
  • Account app-wide, consent per folder. One OpenAI sign-in for the app. Consent, command network, role, and mode stay bound to the chat\'s folder and say so.
  • No Documents tab. There is no surface switch at all. Documents open in the right panel from the file tree, from a reference in a reply, or from an activity row.
  • Workbench and Pipeline retired. Gone from the navigator and the viewport. Their code stays in the tree, unmounted.
  • Document viewer that drags and expands. The divider drags between 280 and about 60% of the window. The expand toggle jumps to a reading width and collapses the left panel to a strip. Pop-out puts the document in its own window. Close returns the panel to Files.
  • Woven in both directions. A reply names a document as a chip; click opens it beside the chat. Select text in the document; "Ask about this" quotes it into the composer with the file and line range attached.
  • Account row pinned to the left panel. Name plus two status dots, OpenAI and local model. Click for the portal popover: sign in or out, consent, the local model switch, Settings, Appearance, About. Settings open in the right panel. Steps 12 to 15.
  • Workbench returns as a view: Workflows. The folder\'s governed workflows in the right panel with role, policy, roadmap position, and next human gate. Opening one steers the chat; the current step shows in the context line. Created from chat with three required declarations: folder, Agent 1 role, delegation policy. Steps 16 to 20; steps 21 to 25 show the rungs reached by proposal.
  • The ladder, prompted. Plain chat, specified chat, governed workflow. The rung is derived from the five-item tuple (folder, agent, permission, delegation, roadmap). Help proposes the second rung and the Agent 1 proposes the third, once, as a card in the dialogue with Accept, Adjust, Not now; the direct route from the context line is the same form. Declines are remembered and recorded.
  • Activity stays a strip. One line at the bottom that says what is happening now. "Details" opens the Activity view in the right panel. No fourth panel.

What "replay" is

The runtime records every session, including the child sessions an agent starts when it delegates. The current shell can load any recorded session as a read-only transcript and calls that a replay lens. Today it hides the primary dialogue to show it, which is what the code comment about "observational siblings" is describing.

In this design there are two cases and neither takes the centre by force. Opening one of your own past chats from the left panel is not a replay at all: it is that chat, in the centre, ready to continue. Opening a child session, one that an agent ran on its own and you cannot type into, is a replay, and it belongs in the right panel as a read-only view with the parent link and a way to widen it. The tertiary panel's drag and expand give it the space it needs when you want to read closely.

The activity strip

Today the shelf is a resizable region from 120 to 480 pixels with three tabs, and it takes that height from the dialogue. The proposal keeps only the strip and moves the detail to the right panel, where it competes with nothing in the centre. Walkthrough steps 7 and 8 show both states.

Recommendation. Build it in this order: centre invariance and the retirement first, then the right panel view switcher with Files and the document viewer, then the references in replies and the quote-to-composer, then the left panel organisation. Each step is usable on its own.

Stone

Resting state. A chat in progress, the right panel on Files, the strip idle. The message box holds only the message; the line under it says where the chat works, with whom, and under what permission. Everything a first-time user needs to understand is in three words: "New chat", the folder, and "Files".

Dialogue · 1180 × 720 · scaled to fit

Left panel: history and navigator for chat

  • Search across chat titles and message text.
  • New chat as the one action at the top, umber plus sign.
  • Pinned, then groups, then by date. Groups are folders you make: drag a chat in, or use "Move to" from its menu. The example group is "Section 8 preservation".
  • Titles from the first message, editable, with the chat\'s folder beneath. Chats from every folder are listed. The runtime id is in the tooltip and nowhere else.
  • Right-click menu: Rename, Pin, Move to, Archive. Delete is in the menu too, with a confirm. Step 9 shows it.

Right panel: one view at a time

  • Files is the default: the working root as a tree. Markdown, text, CSV, JSON, images, and PDF open in-app. Anything else shows a "Reveal in Finder" row instead of a viewer.
  • Workflows lists the folder\'s governed workflows and the templates it qualifies for. Opening one shows its roadmap; Follow steers the chat.
  • Who is working lists the live session and its children with status. Clicking a child opens its replay here.
  • Activity is the full log: tools, events, children. The strip at the bottom is its summary.
  • Document and Session appear as a breadcrumb over whichever view they came from, with a back arrow, so the tab row never grows.
  • Four controls top right, always the same: menu, pop out, expand, close.

Walkthrough

Twenty-six states, one after another. The umber ring marks what was clicked to reach the next state. Use the list, the buttons, or the arrow keys.

    Activity, replay, and the document viewer

    Does the strip expand?

    Today, yes: it is a resizable region with tabs and it pushes the dialogue up. I propose it does not. It stays one line that answers "what is happening right now": the running action, counts, elapsed time. "Details" switches the right panel to Activity. The strip is a status bar; the panel is the log. That keeps the centre's height stable while an agent works, which matters more than it sounds because the composer is where your eyes are.

    A fourth panel would be the same information in a fourth place. If the log needs more room than the right panel gives it, expand the panel, the same gesture as for a document.

    Replay

    Your own chats are not replays. Selecting one in the left panel puts it in the centre and you keep going. A child session, one an agent ran for itself, is read-only and opens in the right panel from Who is working or from the Activity log. It shows the parent link, the persona, what it did, and its transcript. It can be widened, expanded, or popped out like a document. Step 8 shows it.

    The four controls

    ⋮ menu
    Reveal in Finder, Copy path, Open in default app, Attach to message, Reload.
    ↗ pop out
    Same viewer in its own window. The panel returns to Files. Useful with two screens. Step 10.
    ⤢ expand
    Panel jumps to a reading width, about 60% of the window; the left panel collapses to a strip; the dialogue stays with its composer. Same button returns. Step 4.
    × close
    Closes the document or session and returns the panel to the view it came from.
    drag
    The divider between the centre and the panel drags from 280px to the expand width. Width is remembered per view. Step 3.

    What opens in-app

    Markdown rendered, with headings as a table of contents in the menu. Plain text, CSV as a table, JSON folded, images, and PDF through the system viewer. Word and Excel files show a preview card with "Open in default app". The rule is simple: if the app cannot show it faithfully, it says so and hands it off rather than showing a broken page.

    Logo

    Decided. The chalk-on-brick drawing, plain and unbordered, is the app icon, the in-app mark, and the corporate logo, replacing LOGO.jpg. The wordmark is Plex Serif in one colour, the dark umber of the squares on light grounds and cream on dark. Nothing else is proposed.

    Corporate lockup

    Mark and wordmark, Plex Serif regular. The gap is a quarter of the mark's height and the wordmark's cap height is just over half of it, so the two read as one object at any scale. Delivered as PNG on transparent and as a self-contained SVG with the wordmark converted to outlines, so it renders identically without the font installed.

    The semibold weight is also in the folder for contexts that need more presence, such as a sign or a slide title. Regular is the default. Both are the weights the app already bundles; no new font file is needed.

    Full-bleed drawing. The six squares are large enough to read at Dock size, and the cool ground separates it from the Finder blue and grey utilities either side.

    Kept for reference: the header no longer carries the icon, only the name. At 22px the drawing reads as six marks and the umber wordmark carries the name; the texture is felt rather than seen, which is the right amount at reading distance.

    Files in generated/: painted-field at 1024 down to 16 plus painted-field.icns and its iconset; macos-painted-field-1024.png; chirality-logo-lockup-400 and -600 as PNG and SVG, each with a -dark variant. Everything else in that folder is superseded and can be deleted.

    Build notes

    What exists and is reused

    • Dialogue. Streaming, interrupt, persona, attachments, per-session drafts, permission requests inline. Unchanged apart from the composer layout and copy.
    • Document viewer. The deliverable roster, the file picker for the control-plane documents, and markdown rendering already exist and are mounted only in the legacy shell and Workbench. They move into the right panel.
    • File tree. Exists, read-only. Rows become buttons that open the file in the panel.
    • Who is working. The recorded agent hierarchy projection exists behind the Agents tab. It moves to the right panel as a view.
    • Activity. The three stream views exist. They move into the panel; the strip becomes a summary of the same events.
    • Replay. The loader, the selection guard, and the lens exist. Only the placement changes.
    • Panel widths, collapse, persisted state. Exist for both side panels and the shelf.

    What is new

    • Centre invariance. Remove the focused-surface branch from the viewport and the Workbench and Pipeline entries from the navigator. Render replay in the panel, not over the dialogue.
    • Right panel view switcher with Files, Who is working, Activity, and the breadcrumb overlay for Document and Session.
    • References in replies. Paths and deliverable ids in assistant text and in tool rows become chips that open the panel. The chip renders from the same markdown pipeline.
    • Quote to composer. Selection in the viewer offers Ask and Attach. Ask inserts a quote block with file and line range; the runtime already accepts attachments by path, so lines are a small extension.
    • Left panel organisation. Titles from the first message, rename, pin, groups, archive, search. Titles and groups are local annotations like the surface tags today, not project truth.
    • Expand and pop-out. Expand is a width preset plus left collapse. Pop-out is an Electron window on the same route with the panel alone.
    • Copy pass. Route subtitle, eyebrows, navigator notes, "Return to primary dialogue", and the coordination disclaimer all go or become tooltips.

    All of it is frontend product change under the shell tranche: Section 8 preservation is owed on merge, and the D-APP-36 render tests that assert the current markup need their expectations updated. The retirement is a mount change, not a deletion, so nothing in the Workbench or Pipeline test suites needs to move.
